newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers propose child support collection system.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers propose child support collection system.

text.p: Calling the U.S. method of collecting billions of dollars of unpaid child support "appalling," two members of Congress on Thursday proposed a bill that would create a new federal collection system.

Representative Henry Hyde, a conservative Republican from Illinois, and Representative Lynn Woolsey, a liberal Democrat from California, teamed up behind a proposal that would replace a fragmented state-based system with a national one linked to the Internal Revenue Service.

The lawmakers, who modified a proposal from last year that was not enacted, acknowledged that many members of Congress would be reluctant to enlarge IRS responsibilities or set up a new federal programme in an era when many responsiblities are being shifted to the states.

"There is a lack of empathy for the IRS, to put it mildly," Hyde said. But he said lawmakers would have to be "deaf, dumb and blind" not to recognise that this was a problem that the IRS would be well-suited to solve.

Support payments would be withheld from paychecks, just like Social Security taxes are. Families without late payment problems could opt out of the payroll-based system, except in cases where the parent with custody of the children, usually the mother, was on welfare.

A General Accounting Office study released this week underscored the states' failure to keep up with deadbeat parents, despite $2.6 billion spent on upgrading state-run programmes over the last 15 years.

The GAO found that states have increased the amount of support being collected, but are not improving the collection rate. Funds are collected in only about one in five cases, and states are getting only about $3.50 for each dollar they spend on collection efforts.

One recent federal study estimated that $39 billion in accumulated unpaid support is due to over 29 million U.S. children. Woolsey estimated that 300,000 mothers and half a million chidren could get off welfare if the child support was paid.

Woolsey herself was on welfare, even though she also had a low-paying job, when her husband left her with three young children 30 years ago. "Had I received the child support the court had ordered, I wouldn't have needed welfare," she said.
